advances: A geometrically increasing slack coordinate cannot produce an all-center pair obstruction when the equality face of the one budget is an integer affine graph over the entire other-coordinate box. This applies to arbitrary nonlinear log-concave factors in those other coordinates. In particular it rules out the supplied single-budget geometric-face family as a max-center counterexample, regardless of its center-average behavior. The proof establishes a pair-score product corollary of the accepted product argument and an exact boundary-center reduction, without multiplying dependent strip and imbalance probabilities. The general one-cut question remains open when the equality face fails the hypotheses below.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. Accepted fact 488f0a583886b5fc supplies canonical definitions and support facts. The proved one-dimensional probability and block estimates in 11cb4cde5378cfcd are used with the explicit normalization and cutoff conversion above; its integral-cap conclusion is not substituted for a pair conclusion.
proof:
We first prove the product pair corollary carefully, since the conclusion stated in 11cb4cde5378cfcd concerns the integral cap score, not \(K\).

For any two product blocks \(f,g\), choose centers \(j_f,j_g\) and cutoffs \(L_f,L_g\). At a product displacement the curvature is the sum of the two block curvatures, and
\[
\min(f_+g_+,f_-g_-)\ge\min(f_+,f_-)\min(g_+,g_-).
\]
Consequently \(B_{(j_f,j_g)}^\Delta(L_f+L_g;f\otimes g)\ge B_{j_f}^\Delta(L_f;f)B_{j_g}^\Delta(L_g;g)\). Since \(1+L_f+L_g\le(1+L_f)(1+L_g)\), maximizing gives \(K(f\otimes g)\ge K(f)K(g)\). Multiplication of a table by a positive constant scales \(K\) and total mass by that constant and leaves its curvatures unchanged. Thus \(2^kK(f)/W_f\) is supermultiplicative over product blocks.

Normalize each factor to a probability table \(\pi_i\). At a chosen coordinate center \(j_i\), use precisely the auxiliary quantities of the proof of 11cb4cde5378cfcd, with subscripts displayed here to distinguish them from the budget vector \(a\):
\[
s_i(z)=\sqrt{\pi_i(j_i+z)\pi_i(j_i-z)},\quad
p_i=\pi_i(j_i),\quad \beta_i=\sum_zs_i(z),\quad
H_i(z)=\log\frac{p_i}{s_i(z)},\quad
\xi_i(z)=\frac12\log\frac{\pi_i(j_i-z)}{\pi_i(j_i+z)}.
\]
The notation map is exact: our \(\xi_i\) is the odd quantity called \(a_i\) in that accepted proof; all of \(s_i,p_i,\beta_i,H_i\) have the same normalization. Let \(Z_i\) be independent with law \(s_i/\beta_i\), put \(\Xi=\sum_i\xi_i(Z_i)\), and set \(\gamma_i=\log(2\beta_i)\). For a block of \(m\) coordinates, the exact identity \(\min(u,v)=\sqrt{uv}\exp(-|\log(u/v)|/2)\) gives, for every \(T\ge0\),
\[
2^m\frac{B_j^\Delta(2T;\bigotimes_i\pi_i)}{1+2T}
=\frac{\exp(\sum_i\gamma_i)}{1+2T}
\mathbb E\!\left[e^{-|\Xi|}\mathbf1_{\{\sum_iH_i(Z_i)\le T\}}\right].
\tag{1}
\]
Here the curvature is exactly \(2\sum_iH_i\), so there is no cutoff renormalization left implicit. In particular, the normalized block pair score is at least
\[
R_j(T):=\frac{\exp(\sum_i\gamma_i)}{2(1+T)}
\mathbb E\!\left[e^{-|\Xi|}\mathbf1_{\{\sum_iH_i(Z_i)\le T\}}\right],
\tag{2}
\]
because \(1+2T\le2(1+T)\). Formula (2) is exactly the normalized reflection lower expression used in equation (4) of the accepted proof after division by \(1+T\). We now use its proved estimates on this expression, not its final integral-cap theorem.

For completeness, these are the required block estimates and their applicability. Factors with maximum atom at least \(1/2\) use a mode; their zero-displacement pair alone gives normalized coefficient at least one. For every remaining factor choose a median and use the accepted parameters \(\eta_i=\log(\beta_i/p_i)\), \(\delta_i=-\log(2p_i)\), and \(q_i=1-e^{-\eta_i}\). A wide block consists of all factors with \(\eta_i>1/5\). If its size is \(m\ge1\), Sections 2 through 5 of 11cb4cde5378cfcd prove \(\sum\gamma_i\ge m/26\); with probability at least \(1/2\) over magnitudes, \(\sum H_i\le T=4m(1+\log4)\) and \(|\xi_i|\le\log(32m)\). Conditional on these magnitudes, its sign lemma gives \(|\Xi|\le\log(32m)\) with probability at least \(1/(m+1)\). Substitution in (2) proves
\[
R_j(T)\ge\frac{e^{m/26}}{128m(m+1)(1+4m(1+\log4))}\ge e^{-29}.
\tag{3}
\]
The last all-integer inequality is proved in Section 5 of that accepted fact.

For the remaining factors partition the ranges of \(\eta_i\) into \((2^{-j}/10,2^{-j}/5]\), \(j\ge0\). For a group of size \(s\), put \(\mu=\sum q_i\). It is dense when \(\mu\ge100(j+1)\). Section 6 of 11cb4cde5378cfcd proves \(\sum\gamma_i\ge3\mu/4\) and a magnitude event of probability at least \(1/4\), on which at most \(4\mu\) coordinates are nonzero, \(\sum H_i\le T=4\mu(j+5)\), and \(|\xi_i|\le\log(32s)\). Its conditional sign lemma therefore gives \(|\Xi|\le\log(32s)\) with probability at least \(1/(4\mu+1)\). Substitution in (2) gives
\[
R_j(T)\ge\frac{e^{3\mu/4}}{256s(4\mu+1)(1+4\mu(j+5))}\ge1.
\tag{4}
\]
The final inequality, including every \(j\ge0\) and every \(\mu\ge100(j+1)\), is the proved estimate (15) of that accepted fact. Combine the non-dense groups into its sparse block. Its estimate (16) gives \(\sum\delta_i<112\), so the central displacement at cutoff zero has normalized weight \(\prod_i(2p_i)=e^{-\sum\delta_i}\ge e^{-112}\). The accepted one-dimensional estimates ensure \(\eta_i>0\) for all remaining factors, so this partition is exhaustive.

There is at most one wide block, every dense block contributes at least one, and the sparse block contributes at least \(e^{-112}\). The pair supermultiplicativity proved above, together with (1)-(4), yields \(2^kK(f)/W_f\ge e^{-141}\ge e^{-150}\). Empty blocks are simply omitted. This proves the pair corollary; it does not infer any inequality from an integral-cap lower bound alone.

We now turn to the one-cut table. Each support \(E_i\) is a finite interval of integers, as proved in 488f0a583886b5fc. The factor \(r^t\mathbf1_{[\ell_-,\ell_+]\cap\mathbb Z}(t)\) has the finite-valued log-concave extension \(r^t\mathbf1_{[\ell_-,\ell_+]}(t)\). Multiply the factor extensions and truncate by the displayed closed halfspace. This is a globally log-concave extension agreeing at every lattice point, including all zeros.

Since \(a\cdot x+t\) and \(b_0\) are integers, the inequality with \(b_0+\theta\), \(0\le\theta<1\), is exactly the inequality with \(b_0\) on the lattice. The complete support is therefore
\[
D=\{(x,t):x\in E,\ t\in\mathbb Z,\ \ell_-\le t\le h(x)\}.
\tag{5}
\]
The assumed lower bound on \(h\) makes every column nonempty, while its upper bound makes the independent upper endpoint \(\ell_+\) inactive in (5). No boundary lattice point is removed.

Define the integer affine map \(F(x)=(x,h(x))\) and the boundary table
\[
f_x:=w_{F(x)}=r^{b_0}\prod_{i=1}^k\bigl(u_i(x_i)r^{-a_ix_i}\bigr)
\quad(x\in\mathbb Z^k).
\tag{6}
\]
Outside \(E\) this formula is zero. Each factor in parentheses is globally extendable log-concave: multiplication by an exponential of an affine function preserves log-concavity and all table zeros. The constant \(r^{b_0}\) can be absorbed into one factor. Thus the pair corollary applies to \(f\).

Fix \(j\in E\) and the feasible center \(J=F(j)\). Write an arbitrary integer displacement as \(v=(z,s)\). Both endpoints can satisfy the budget only if
\[
b_0+(a\cdot z+s)\le b_0,\qquad
b_0-(a\cdot z+s)\le b_0,
\]
which is equivalent to \(s=-a\cdot z\). This is an integer displacement precisely as written because \(a\) is integral. Conversely, for every \(z\in\mathbb Z^k\) with \(j\pm z\in E\), the endpoints \(J\pm(z,-a\cdot z)=F(j\pm z)\) both lie in (5), by the height hypothesis. Hence \(z\mapsto(z,-a\cdot z)\) is a bijection from all positive reflected displacements of \(f\) at \(j\) onto all positive reflected displacements of \(w\) at \(F(j)\). It preserves both orientations, zero, both endpoint weights, the center weight, and therefore every curvature. For every \(L\ge0\) this proves the exact identities
\[
B_{F(j)}^\Delta(L;w)=B_j^\Delta(L;f),\qquad
K_{F(j)}(w)=K_j(f).
\tag{7}
\]
In particular \(K(w)\ge K(f)\). The strip is satisfied identically for these pairs; no probabilistic independence between strip and imbalance is asserted.

Finally, summing each full column in (5) gives
\[
W=\sum_{x\in E}f_x\sum_{d=0}^{h(x)-\ell_-}r^{-d}
\le\frac{1}{1-r^{-1}}\sum_{x\in E}f_x
=\frac{W_f}{1-r^{-1}}.
\tag{8}
\]
All sums are finite; the infinite geometric sum is used only for the upper bound. Equations (7), (8), and the product pair corollary imply \(K(w)\ge e^{-150}2^{-k}(1-r^{-1})W\). Since \(n=k+1\), this is the asserted bound.

In the stated geometric example, \(h(x)=kM-\sum_i x_i\) lies in \([0,kM]\) for every \(x\in E\); all theorem hypotheses hold. Since \(r=4^k\ge4\), the coefficient \(2(1-r^{-1})\) is at least \(3/2\), proving its claimed uniform bound.

This is a statement about the pair score \(K\). It neither identifies \(K\) with the original-weight integral logarithmic hitting score of 488f0a583886b5fc nor supplies a counterexample to the locked mixed-integer depth target. The excluded mechanism is exactly the one described in the statement; an arbitrary oblique cut can have a boundary with no such complete integer graph.
statement:
Use the canonical notation of accepted fact 488f0a583886b5fc: for a finite globally extendable table, \(D=\{I:w_I>0\}\), \(W=\sum_Iw_I\), \(\phi_I=\log(w_{\max}/w_I)\), and \(B=\max_D\phi\). At \(J\in D\), let \(\mathcal U_J=\{v\in\mathbb Z^n:w_{J+v}w_{J-v}>0\}\), \(\Delta_J(v)=\log(w_J^2/(w_{J+v}w_{J-v}))\), and
\[
B_J^\Delta(L)=\sum_{\substack{v\in\mathcal U_J\\\Delta_J(v)\le L}}
\min(w_{J+v},w_{J-v}),\qquad
K_J(w)=\max_{L\ge0}\frac{B_J^\Delta(L)}{1+L},\qquad K(w)=\max_{J\in D}K_J(w).
\]
All displacement sums are oriented and include zero exactly once. The unadorned \(B\) is only the potential range; the superscripted \(B_J^\Delta\) is the canonical pair numerator. All logarithms are natural.

First, the following pair-score consequence of the reflection proof in accepted fact 11cb4cde5378cfcd holds. If \(f\) is any product of \(k\ge1\) finite nonzero globally extendable one-dimensional log-concave factors, and \(W_f=\sum_xf_x\), then \(K(f)\ge e^{-150}2^{-k}W_f\), using the same pair definition in dimension \(k\).

Now fix \(k\ge1\), put \(n=k+1\), and let \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\) be any such one-dimensional factors. Write their positive support intervals as \(E_i\), and set \(E=\prod_i E_i\). Fix integers \(\ell_-\le\ell_+\), \(b_0\in\mathbb Z\), a vector \(a\in\mathbb Z^k\), a real \(0\le\theta<1\), and a real \(r>1\). Assume
\[
\ell_-\le h(x):=b_0-a\cdot x\le\ell_+\qquad(x\in E).
\]
The alias \(h\) here is the displayed affine slack height, not any height or potential from a predecessor. On every integer site \((x,t)\in\mathbb Z^k\times\mathbb Z\), define
\[
w_{(x,t)}=\left(\prod_{i=1}^k u_i(x_i)\right)r^t
\mathbf1_{\{\ell_-\le t\le\ell_+\}}
\mathbf1_{\{a\cdot x+t\le b_0+\theta\}}.
\]
This is a product of \(n\) finite globally extendable one-dimensional log-concave factors truncated by exactly one halfspace. Then
\[
\frac{2^nK(w)}{W}\ge 2(1-r^{-1})e^{-150}.
\]
In particular the right-hand side is at least \(e^{-150}\) when \(r\ge2\).

For the explicit family \(M=(k+1)^2\), \(r=4^k\), \(q=k/(k+1)\), \(E_i=\{0,\ldots,M\}\), \(u_i(s)=(rq)^s\mathbf1_{E_i}(s)\), \(\ell_-=0\), \(\ell_+=kM\), \(a=(1,\ldots,1)\), and \(b_0=kM\), this gives \(2^{k+1}K(w)/W\ge(3/2)e^{-150}\) for every \(k\ge1\) and every \(0\le\theta<1\). No assertion about its center average is needed or used.
